claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The alloy was produced by selective laser melting.
Rapid solidification leaves inherent grain-boundary microsegregation in the as-built alloy.
Al and Ti are preferentially segregated at grain boundaries in the as-built alloy.
Grain-boundary segregation of reactive elements promotes preferential oxidation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases.
Reactive-element segregation causes heterogeneous oxide-scale formation.
Heterogeneous oxide scales compromise degradation resistance.
Post-build heat treatment can minimize grain-boundary segregation.
Grain-boundary chemical gradients drive localized formation of non-uniform and sometimes defective oxide scales.
Microsegregated grain-boundary zones oxidize faster during high-temperature redox cycling.
Localized aggressive oxidation produces uneven oxide-layer development.
Heat-treated samples with reduced segregation will form more uniform oxide scales than the as-built baseline.
Heat-treated samples with reduced segregation will form more adherent oxide scales than the as-built baseline.
Heat-treated samples will degrade more slowly than the as-built baseline.
Slower degradation will be evidenced by lower mass change and reduced microcrack density.
The as-built baseline has pronounced grain-boundary segregation, heterogeneous oxide-scale formation, and faster degradation during redox exposure.
The proposed segregation-controlled mechanism operates between 750 and 900 degrees Celsius in controlled oxidizing or reducing atmospheres.
Outside 750–900 degrees Celsius, additional degradation phenomena may dominate.
